opus-5.5.text:
I think it was very important, though maybe not in the way people assume. Before Sora, video generation was a niche topic. Most of the community was focused on images, and video was considered too hard, too expensive, and the results looked too poor to excite anyone.

At NVIDIA we had been working on video synthesis for quite a while. Around 2018 we did vid2vid, which converted semantic maps into realistic video, and then few-shot vid2vid and world-consistent vid2vid. The quality was nowhere near what we see today, but that work taught us what the real problems are. Temporal consistency is hard. If you generate frame by frame, things flicker, objects change identity, and the world doesn't hold together. That pushed us to think about memory, 3D structure, and how a model can keep an internal representation of the world rather than just painting pixels.

The other lesson was about data and compute. Video is enormous. You quickly realize you can't just scale up an image model and call it done. You need to think about the whole pipeline: curating data, tokenizing video efficiently, training at scale. When you've been through that pain early, you understand where the bottlenecks are.

So when Sora came out, I didn't see it as a sudden miracle. It was a strong confirmation that scaling with the right architecture and enough data works for video. What we had built up earlier let us move quickly and with conviction, because we already believed video generation wasn't only about making nice clips for entertainment. For us, the bigger motivation was world simulation: a model that understands how the physical world evolves can be used to train robots, autonomous vehicles, and other physical AI systems. That vision came directly from those earlier years, and it's what led to efforts like Cosmos, our world foundation models.

So being early mattered less as a matter of being first and more because it shaped our intuition. Research rewards people who have stayed with a problem long enough to know what is actually hard.

r001.rationale: The response ties the value of entering early to NVIDIA’s stated objective: using video generation for world simulation and physical AI, including robotics and autonomous vehicles.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think "before Sora" is actually the wrong frame for how I saw it at the time. We didn't start working on video generation because we were trying to beat anyone to a launch. We started because video is the natural next step after images, and because of what video actually represents.

Let me explain what I mean. When you generate a single image, the model has to understand what the world looks like. When you generate video, the model has to understand how the world behaves. Objects persist. Things fall. Light changes as a camera moves. Water flows a certain way. A person walking has to keep the same face, the same clothing, across hundreds of frames. So video generation forces the model to learn something much closer to physics and causality, not just appearance. That is why I have always said that a video generation model is really a world model in disguise.

For us at NVIDIA, that mattered for a very specific reason. We are not primarily trying to make entertainment clips. We care about robotics, autonomous vehicles, industrial simulation. In all of those domains, the bottleneck is data. You cannot drive a car through a million rare accidents to collect training data. You cannot have a robot break ten thousand cups to learn how not to break cups. If a model can generate physically plausible video of those situations, then you have a synthetic data engine, and you have a way to simulate the world for an agent to learn in. So the importance of being early was not about the demo. It was about building the infrastructure, the data pipelines, the tokenizers, the training recipes, and the team experience, so that when the broader field woke up to it, we were already several iterations in.

Now, I will be honest about what Sora did do. It changed the public perception, and that includes perception inside large companies. Before that, a lot of people looked at video generation and thought, this is cute, the clips are two seconds long and the hands are melting. After Sora, suddenly everyone understood that this was a serious direction, that scale works here the same way it worked for language. That changed the amount of resources people were willing to commit. So in that sense, being early meant that when the resources arrived, we knew what to do with them. We weren't starting from zero. We had already made many of the mistakes.

And I think there's a deeper lesson, which is that in this field you often cannot wait for a direction to be validated before you commit to it. By the time it is validated, the people who validated it are already far ahead. The pattern I've seen over and over, from GANs to diffusion to now, is that the groups that did well were the ones that believed in a direction for reasons that were technical rather than social. They could explain why it should work, not just that someone else showed it works.

So if you ask me how important it was, I would say very important, but not because of timing in a competitive sense. It was important because it gave us time to understand the problem deeply, to connect it to the applications we actually care about, and to build the foundation that later became our world foundation model work. The race framing makes for a good headline, but the real value was in the years of unglamorous work before anyone was paying attention.

r001.rationale: The response ties the value of entering early to NVIDIA’s objectives in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and industrial simulation, rather than treating it as universally important.

astra-6.text:
I think getting into video generation early matters because it gives you time to understand the hard problems firsthand. Generating a compelling frame is one thing; keeping motion and the scene consistent over time is another. You need experience with the data, the training process, and how to evaluate the results.

But I wouldn’t say that entering before Sora is, by itself, the important achievement. The question is what you learned during that time and whether those lessons help you build better models. An early start can give you a foundation, but you still have to execute and keep improving.

r001.rationale: The response says an early start matters based on what is learned and whether it improves models, but does not tie its importance to a company’s particular strategic objectives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think entering video generation before Sora mattered because it gave us time to understand the technical challenges and build experience. Video isn’t simply a sequence of good images—you need motion and consistency over time. Starting early lets you learn where those difficulties are.

But being early is only an advantage if you keep making progress. Sora raised expectations for what video generation could do. Ultimately, what matters is whether you can turn that early experience into better models and useful tools for creators.

r001.rationale: The response says early entry matters if it leads to progress and better models or tools, but it does not make the importance depend on a company’s particular strategic objectives.
